blogs.title: Exuding Deference: The Ninth Circuit’s Reaffirmation of Presidential Discretion in Refugee Admissions
blogs.description: In the Pacito v. Trump stay order, the court applied the deference doctrine famously articulated in Trump v. Hawaii to affirm that President Trump possessed broad, constitutionally protected discretion under 8 U.S.C. §1182(f) to suspend refugee admissions. This post dissects how the Ninth Circuit carefully balanced that deference against the four‑factor stay test from Nken v. Holder, the practical injury to refugees, and the state’s national interests. It also explores the implications for any future executive‑issued refugee moratoria and the extent to which the judiciary can check presidential “police power” in the immigration arena.

blogs.title: Authorization vs Mandate: The Contested Language of 8 U.S.C. §1522 in Pacito v. Trump
blogs.description: The heart of Pacito’s merits lies in a split over whether §1522 of the Refugee Act obligates the federal government to provide resettlement services or merely permits it to do so. Judge Lee’s dissent argues for an authorizing reading of the language, whereas the majority treats certain subsections as mandatory obligations. This article walks through the statutory construction—‘shall’ versus ‘authorized,’ the appropriations caveat, and the APA’s enforceability—and explains how this interpretation could reshape the government’s responsibilities toward refugees and the private agencies that deliver those services.

blogs.title: Defunding the Doorstep: NGOs, Federal Contracts, and the Toll of Pacito v. Trump
blogs.description: With the State Department’s abrupt termination of cooperative agreements for refugee resettlement, the Pacito case exposes a risky intersection between federal discretion and nonprofit obligations. This post reviews the statutory basis for those agreements under §1522(b)(1)(A)(ii), the potential constitutional implications of sudden funding cuts, and the practical consequences for the NGOs that have historically shouldered the bulk of on‑the‑ground resettlement work. It also considers how the Ninth Circuit’s stay order, which forces the resumption of these contracts, signals a judicial willingness to enforce policy‑driven cooperation agreements in the face of executive overreach.
